newsitem.title: USA: CIA nominee vows to draw more on private sector.
newsitem.headline: CIA nominee vows to draw more on private sector.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to lead the CIA into the 21st century, George Tenet, vowed on Tuesday to close the door on the Cold War and draw more frequently on expertise in the U.S. private sector.

"Ultimately, leadership at this moment means closing the door on the Cold War and embracing the challenges and opportunities of the new era," he said in an opening statement to the Senate Intelligence Committee, which is considering his nomination.
"I would turn our gaze from the past, fix our attention on the future and target our investments on innovation," he added.

If confirmed, "I would insist that we draw more frequently on the expertise that resides in our country's private sector by sponsoring more scholars in residence and reaching out to specialists who can help us fill critical gaps," Tenet said.

The son of a Greek immigrant father who owned a diner in the New York City borough of Queens, Tenet, 44, would be the fifth director of central intelligence in six years and the third to serve under Clinton.
He has held the the intelligence community's second-ranking post since July 1995 and served as acting chief U.S. spymaster since John Deutch left in December after 20 months in the job.
Clinton tapped Tenet for the job after a bruising fight with Senate Republicans over the abortive nomination of Anthony Lake, the president's first-term national security adviser.
In withdrawing his name on March 17, Lake denounced the confirmation process, which he described in a letter to the president as "nasty and brutish without being short."

Unlike Lake, an easy target for Clinton foreign policy critics, Tenet appeared a shoo-in to be confirmed as the 18th director of central intelligence since the modern U.S. espionage bureaucracy took shape 50 years ago.

Committee Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, has called Tenet "a man of integrity and professionalism." The panel's vice chairman, Bob Kerrey, a Democrat from Nebraska, said on Tuesday that Tenet had been able "to demonstrate his merit."
Tenet is a former staff director of the Intelligence Committee who later became senior intelligence adviser on the White House National Security Council staff under Lake.
If confirmed, Tenet would not only run the CIA but oversee the 12 other U.S. spy agencies that together employ tens of thousands of people and spend about $30 billion a year.
He would be Clinton's third chief spymaster after Deutch and James Woolsey, who quit in December 1994 after becoming entangled in the case of convicted CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames.
